items.prose: A grain trader is short a forward on one tonne of wheat at $F = \text{£}120.00$. At delivery wheat trades at £135.00.
items.question: What is the trader's payoff?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The short's payoff is $F - S_T$.

byKey.long: You used the long's payoff. The short must sell wheat worth £135.00 for £120.00.
byKey.floor: You gave the forward a floor. The short is bound to deliver, so the loss stands.

explain.text: The short delivers wheat worth £135.00 and receives £120.00, a payoff of −£15.00. The long gains exactly that.

items.prose: A share trades at £80.00 and pays no dividends. The rate is 3% a year, compounded yearly.
items.question: What is the no-arbitrage two-year forward price? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Grow £80.00 at 3% for two years.

byKey.simple: You used simple interest, $80 \times 1.06$. The financing compounds.
byKey.one: That is the one-year forward. Delivery is in two years.
byKey.spot: You left out the cost of carry. Holding the share for two years costs interest.

explain.text: Borrowing £80.00 for two years repays $80 \times 1.03^2 = \text{£}84.872$. That is what delivering the share costs, so $F = \text{£}84.87$.

items.prose: A share trades at £100.00 with no dividends, and the one-year rate is 5%. A dealer quotes the one-year forward at £110.00.
items.question: What riskless profit per share can you lock in, received at delivery?

feedback.correct: Deliver for £110.00 a share that costs £105.00 to carry: £5.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Borrow, buy and sell forward; compare the £110.00 with what the loan repays.

byKey.vs-spot: You compared the quote with today's price. Buying the share needs a loan that grows to £105.00.
byKey.pv: That is the profit's value today. The question asks what you receive at delivery.

explain.text: Borrow £100.00, buy the share, sell it forward at £110.00. At delivery you receive £110.00 and repay £105.00, keeping £5.00 whatever the share does.

items.prose: You are long 3 index futures at £10.00 a point. The initial margin is £6,000.00 a contract and the maintenance margin £4,500.00 a contract. Your account holds £18,000.00. Today the future falls 200 points.
items.question: How large is the margin call?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the loss on all 3 contracts, the new balance, and the gap to the initial margin.

byKey.maint: You topped up to the maintenance level, £13,500.00. A call restores the initial margin, £18,000.00.
byKey.one: That is one contract's loss. You hold 3.
byKey.none: £12,000.00 is below 3 times £4,500.00, so a call is due.

explain.text: The loss is $3 \times 200 \times 10 = \text{£}6{,}000.00$, leaving £12,000.00. That is below the £13,500.00 maintenance level, so you pay £6,000.00 to restore £18,000.00.

items.prose: You short 300 shares at £15.00 and cover at £18.00. The stock loan fee is £20.00, and no dividend is paid.
items.question: What is your profit? Use a negative number for a loss.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $P_0 - P_1 - C$ per trade.

byKey.fee-helped: You took the fee off the loss. A fee always makes the result worse.
byKey.sign: The share rose against your short, so this is a loss.

explain.text: Covering at £18.00 costs £3.00 a share more than the sale raised: £900.00 on 300 shares. With the £20.00 fee the loss is £920.00.

items.prose: A position has leverage $L = 4$, borrowing at 5% a year. Over the year the asset returns −10%.
items.question: What is the return on equity?

widget.placeholder: a percentage; negative for a loss
widget.label: Return on equity

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $R_E = L R_A - (L - 1) r$.

byKey.no-int: You scaled the fall but forgot the interest on three units of borrowing.
byKey.int-once: You charged interest on one unit. With $L = 4$ you borrow three times your equity.
byKey.unlev: That is the asset's return. Your equity moves four times as much.

explain.text: $R_E = 4 \times (-0.10) - 3 \times 0.05 = -0.55$. The 10% fall costs 40% of equity, and the interest another 15%.

items.prose: Four positions, each held to the delivery or expiry date. Ignore any premium paid.
items.question: Select all that apply: which positions can lose without limit?

options.text: A short sale of a share

options.why: A long forward loses at most $F$, if the asset goes to zero.
A long call's payoff never falls below zero; the most you lose is the premium.

feedback.correct: The short forward and the short sale both lose as the price rises, without limit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which positions lose when the price rises, and whether prices have a ceiling.

explain.text: Both short positions lose £1.00 for each £1.00 the price rises, and prices have no ceiling. A long forward's worst case is the asset going to zero. A call has a floor at zero.

items.prose: A share trades at £60.00. It pays a £1.50 dividend in three months. The rate is 4% a year, compounded yearly.
items.question: What is the no-arbitrage one-year forward price? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the dividend's present value off £60.00, then grow for a year.

byKey.ignored: You left out the dividend. The holder receives £1.50 that the forward's buyer does not.
byKey.not-grown: You took £1.50 off £62.40. Received at three months, it earns interest for nine more: £1.545.
byKey.not-disc: You took the full £1.50 off today's price. Paid in three months, it is worth £1.485 today.

items.prose: You hold £30,000.00 of shares bought with £12,000.00 of your own money and an £18,000.00 margin loan. The broker requires equity of at least 30% of the position's value.
items.question: Below what position value does the broker sell? Give two decimal places.

widget.label: Position value at the forced sale

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write equity as $V - 18{,}000$ and set it equal to 30% of $V$.

byKey.orig: You took 30% of the original £30,000.00 as the trigger for your equity. The rule uses the value now.
byKey.zero: That is where your equity is gone. The broker sells earlier, at 30%.
byKey.of-loan: You measured 30% of the loan. The rule is 30% of the position's value, $V$.

explain.text: Equity is $V - 18{,}000$; the rule needs $V - 18{,}000 \ge 0.3V$, so $V \ge \tfrac{18{,}000}{0.7} = 25{,}714.29$. A fall of only 14.3% triggers it, because the position starts at 2.5 times leverage.
